<div class="post-wrap">

  <!-- ── Header ── -->
  <header class="post-header">
    <p class="post-description">
      <strong>TL;DR</strong> We propose a simple method to unlock the value of failed agent trajectories—extracting their factual mistakes, 
      injecting them as privileged information in user prompts as inoculation, and achieving <strong>4.1% gain on SWE-bench Verified with under 4.5K trajectories with the Qwen3-32B-Instruct model</strong>.
    </p>
  </header>

  <!-- ── TL;DR ── -->
  <div class="tldr-box">
    <span class="tldr-label">Abstract</span>
    Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of language models for coding agents typically relies exclusively on positive trajectories when the training data are distilled from stronger teacher models [Microsoft AI, 2026]. 
    This leaves a vast amount of available data<strong>—failed trajectories—</strong>completely unused, 
    despite the fact that they often contain partially correct reasoning and valuable intermediate action steps. 
    In this post, we experiment with <em>a simple method to recycle the negative trajectories by extracting the factual mistakes negative trajectories encode</em>. 
    Given a problem statement, a failed trajectory, and a gold patch, we first ask an LLM to extract errors made by the agent in the trajectory and then inject them as Privileged Information (PI)
    into the user prompt. By integrating incorrect information found in the trajectory in the user prompt during SFT, the model will tend to attend to the incorrect information rather than storing in the weights, thus achieving an effect similar to inoculation prompting [Wichers et al., 2025]. 
    By integrating these failed trajectories into agent training, we achieve a <strong>4.1% improvement</strong> over positive-only SFT baselines on the Qwen3-32B-Instruct model and a <strong>2.8% improvement</strong> on the Qwen3-4B-Instruct model with <strong>under 4.5K</strong> and <strong>37K</strong> total trajectories, respectively, on SWE-bench Verified. 
  </div>

  <div style="text-align: center; margin: 1.5rem 0 0.5rem;">
    <img src="{{ 'figures/negativepi/pi_overview.png' | relative_url }}" alt="PI training overview" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;" />  
  </div>

  <!-- ── Failed Trajectories Aren't Uniformly Bad ── -->
  <h2 style="margin-top: 1rem;">Failed Trajectories Aren’t Uniformly Bad</h2>

  <p>When training small language models to act as coding agents, the standard recipe is straightforward: collect successful trajectories from a larger teacher model, filter for the ones that reach the correct solution, and fine-tune on those. This pipeline discards a large fraction of the data: negative trajectories. Furthermore, scaling this pipeline to collect more data requires multiple inference attempts just to accumulate a sufficient positive pool.</p>

  <p>On the other hand, training on failures naively can teach the model the wrong behaviors, and it's not obvious how to separate useful signal from noise in a trajectory that receives negative reward. So most work simply doesn't use negative trajectories at all.</p>

  <p>However, a failed trajectory is not uniformly bad. It might contain a correct file localization step, a reasonable hypothesis about the bug, and then one wrong edit that breaks everything. The trajectory fails, but most of what happened before that wrong turn is still worth learning from. The question is how to make that explicit to the model during training.</p>

  <p>Our approach is simple: for each negative trajectory, we ask another model to extract specific facts—the mistaken beliefs the agent acted on—and inject them into the user prompt as explicitly labeled wrong knowledge. 
    When we recycle negative trajectories for SFT, we include the wrong facts in the context of that trajectory so that the model is aware of what it did wrong: 
    <em>here is what is wrong in the current trajectory.</em> This is the "privileged information"—derived from the gold patch and available only at training time, not at inference. It primes the model with knowledge of what was wrongly inferred, so it can more easily learn from the rest.</p>

  <!-- ── Method ── -->
  <h2>How We Recycle Negative Trajectories</h2>

  <p>Our setup involves supervised fine-tuning a Qwen3-32B-Instruct model 
    on teacher model (MiniMax M2.5)'s trajectories. To establish a baseline, we first train a 32B model solely on the teacher's positive trajectories from the SWE-Rebench dataset. 
    Then, we train another 32B model on both positive and negative trajectories, where the negative trajectories are augmented with the privileged information about what was wrong.
    Our approach yields a <strong>4.1% improvement</strong>, achieving <strong>58.05 on SWE-bench Verified with under 4.5K trajectories</strong> on Qwen3-32B-Instruct model. Our approach also yields a <strong>2.8% improvement</strong> on the Qwen3-4B-Instruct model with <strong>under 37K total trajectories</strong>.</p>

  <h3>How we utilize negative trajectories</h3>

  <div style="text-align: center; margin: 0.5rem 0;">
    <img src="{{ 'figures/negativepi/stepwise%20overview.png' | relative_url }}" alt="Four-step overview of summarization, verification, filtering and data construction, and supervised fine-tuning" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;" />  
  </div>
  <div class="step-block" style="margin-top: 0.75rem;">
    <span class="step-label">Step 1 — Summarization</span>
    We take reward-0 (failed) trajectories and use an LLM to summarize the trajectory in Markdown format. Each summary captures structured information about the trajectory, including sections like <code>#Root Cause</code>, <code>#Key Code Locations</code>, <code>#Fix Applied</code>, and <code>#Fix Strategies</code>.
  </div>

  <div class="step-block">
    <span class="step-label">Step 2 — Verification</span>
    We treat each line of the summary as an atomic fact and run LLM-based fact verification on each line with the information from the gold patch. 
    The LLM receives the summary, trajectory, problem statement, and gold patch, and outputs a verified label—<strong>True</strong>, <strong>Wrong</strong>, or <strong>Uncertain</strong>—along with a justification, <em>i.e., hint/evidence</em> of the label.
  </div>

  <p>Here is a real example of a labeled wrong fact:</p>

  <div class="callout-box">
    <div class="callout-row">
      <span class="callout-label label-wrong">Wrong</span>
      <span class="callout-line">[WRONG] 3. <strong>Fix:</strong> Instead of calling <code>.format()</code> on the holes collection, compute the hole ranges directly.</span>
      <span class="callout-evidence"><em>evidence/hint:</em> The gold patch fixes this differently: it checks if <code>'{holes}'</code> is in the pattern before computing holes, and similarly for <code>'{range}'</code>/<code>'{ranges}'</code>. The agent's approach of inlining holes computation differs from the gold patch.</span>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="step-block">
    <span class="step-label">Step 3 — Filtering, Preprocessing &amp; Data Construction</span>
    We filter for lines labeled <em>Wrong</em>, remove the evidence/hint annotations, and construct a new set of negative trajectory training examples with these wrong facts listed in the user prompt.
  </div>

  <p>Below is the structure of the privileged-information block added to user prompts in the training data. During the evaluation, we remove the &lt;information&gt; block.</p>

  <div class="prompt-block">
    <span class="comment">I also provide some information in &lt;information&gt; gathered from previous</span><br>
    <span class="comment">exploration attempts on this same problem by other agents. Note that this</span><br>
    <span class="comment">information has been verified to contain only incorrect facts — these are</span><br>
    <span class="comment">things that were tried and confirmed to be wrong.</span><br>
    <br>
    <span class="tag">&lt;information&gt;</span><br>
    <br>
    &nbsp;&nbsp;## Key Code Locations<br>
    <br>
    &nbsp;<span class="wrong">[WRONG] - **`CUSTOM_ENV_RE` regex**: `/testbed/k8s_handle/config.py:16`</span><br>
    &nbsp;<span class="comment">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;- Original regex that only matches one env pattern per string</span><br>
    &nbsp;<span class="wrong">[WRONG] - **`_SINGLE_ENV_RE` regex**: `/testbed/k8s_handle/config.py:18`</span><br>
    &nbsp;<span class="comment">&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;- New regex added to match a single env pattern anywhere in a string</span><br>
    <br>
    <span class="tag">&lt;/information&gt;</span><br>
    <br>
    <span class="note">IMPORTANT notes about the &lt;information&gt; section:</span><br>
    <span class="note">- All entries are confirmed wrong facts or failed directions from previous agents.</span><br>
    <span class="note">- Use this to avoid repeating the same mistakes, but do not use it as a guide</span><br>
    <span class="note">&nbsp;&nbsp;for what to try.</span>
  </div>

  <div class="step-block">
    <span class="step-label">Step 4 — SFT</span>
    We mix these augmented negative trajectories with positive trajectories as a training dataset and train via standard SFT.
  </div>


  <div style="text-align: center; margin: 1.5rem 0 0.5rem;">
  <img src="data:image/gif;base64," alt="PI training animation" style="max-width:100%;height:auto;" />  
  </div>



  <!-- ── Why Negative ── -->
  <h2>Why Do Negative Trajectories Help?</h2>

  <h3>Couldn't this just be that we train on more data?</h3>

  <p>To rule this out, we scaled the positive-only data from 3.7K to 15K trajectories. 
    Pass@1 plateaued at the 3.7K baseline (pass@3 improved only marginally), so 11K 
    additional positive trajectories yielded no measurable gain on pass@1. By contrast, 
    adding just 0.7K negative trajectories to the 3.7K baseline lifted both pass@1 and 
    pass@3 to the 15K positive trajectory level. A small amount of negative data matched what a
    large amount of extra positive data could not.</p>

  <div class="table-wrap">
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr><th></th><th>Avg Pass@1</th><th>Pass@3</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>3.7K positive trajectories</td><td>53.95 ± 1.83</td><td>67.6</td></tr>
        <tr class="highlight-row"><td><strong>+ 0.7K negative trajectories</strong></td><td class="bold-row"><strong>58.05 ± 1.10</strong></td><td class="bold-row"><strong>70.4</strong></td></tr>
        <tr><td>15K positive trajectories</td><td>54.10 ± 0.71</td><td>70.0</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <h3>Could it be diversity—more unique tasks?</h3>

  <p>Since negative trajectories cover tasks the positive set didn't, the gains might come 
    from added task diversity rather than the negatives themselves. But the matched-task 
    comparison rules this out: adding 0.7K negative trajectories (→54.50) matches adding 
    1K positive ones (→53.95) on pass@1 and beats them on pass@3 (68.40 vs 67.6)—more 
    gain from fewer examples. The effect is starker at scale: 0.7K negatives lift the 3.7K-positive base 
    by 4.1% (→58.05), while growing the positive set from 3.7K to 15K adds just 
    0.15 (→54.1). So the two sources of signal aren't equivalent—failed trajectories 
    carry information positives don't: what went wrong. If we simply train on raw negatives, 
    this signal comes with a risk: training on failures can nudge the 
    model toward the mistakes it should avoid. Labeling the wrong facts explicitly in the 
    prompt (privileged information) mitigates this, letting the model learn what 
    to avoid rather than imitating it.</p>

  <div class="table-wrap">
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr><th>Configuration</th><th>Dataset Size</th><th>Unique Tasks</th><th>Avg Pass@1</th><th>Pass@3</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>2.7K positive</td><td>2,707</td><td>2,701</td><td>50.93 ± 0.12</td><td>67.0</td></tr>
        <tr class="highlight-row"><td><strong>2.7K positive + 0.7K negative</strong></td><td>3,407</td><td>3,398</td><td class="bold-row"><strong>54.50 ± 0.10</strong></td><td class="bold-row"><strong>68.4</strong></td></tr>
        <tr><td>3.7K positive</td><td>3,717</td><td>3,717</td><td>53.95 ± 1.83</td><td>67.6</td></tr>
        <tr class="highlight-row"><td><strong>3.7K positive + 0.7K negative</strong></td><td>4,407</td><td>4,407</td><td class="bold-row"><strong>58.05 ± 1.10</strong></td><td class="bold-row"><strong>70.4</strong></td></tr>
        <tr><td>15K positive</td><td>14,536</td><td>4,886</td><td>54.10 ± 0.71</td><td>70.0</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <!-- ── PI Ablation ── -->
  <h2>Does Privileged Information Help?</h2>

  <p>To isolate the effect of privileged information (PI), we compare three training configurations: 
    a baseline trained on positive trajectories only, a variant augmented with negative trajectories 
    but <em>without</em> PI, and our full method that pairs negative trajectories with PI.</p>

  <div class="table-wrap">
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr><th>Configuration</th><th>Avg Pass@1</th><th>Pass@3</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Positive trajectories only</td><td>53.95 ± 1.83</td><td>67.6</td></tr>
        <tr><td>+ Negative trajectories (no PI)</td><td>56.67 ± 1.37</td><td>69.6</td></tr>
        <tr class="highlight-row"><td><strong>+ Negative trajectories (with PI)</strong></td><td class="bold-row"><strong>58.05 ± 1.10</strong></td><td class="bold-row"><strong>70.4</strong></td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <p>Adding negative 
    trajectories without PI lifts Pass@1 from 53.95 to 56.67—the diversity and 
    failure-signal benefit we saw earlier, captured even from raw negatives. Pairing 
    them with PI reaches 58.05, isolating the additional contribution of labeling what 
    went wrong. Marking the wrong facts in the user prompt lets the model treat the 
    failed actions as conditioned on that flawed context rather than as behavior to 
    imitate, so it internalizes the mistakes less even while still learning from negative trajectories. 
    The full 4.1% gain over the positive-only baseline has 
    non-overlapping error bars, so it isn't seed noise; the raw→PI step (56.67 → 58.05) 
    is smaller and within error bars but points the same direction and is echoed on 
    Pass@3 (69.6 → 70.4). Pass@3 rises consistently across all three settings 
    (67.6 → 69.6 → 70.4), suggesting negative trajectories don't just raise average 
    accuracy but broaden the set of problems the model can solve given a few attempts—a 
    property we'd expect to give RL a richer reward signal to work with.</p>


  <!-- ── Quality ── -->
  <h2>Are All Negative Trajectories Equally Helpful?</h2>

  <p>Unlike positive trajectories used in SFT training, negative trajectories inherently exhibit greater variance in quality. 
    Some may have followed the right problem-solving strategy overall, only receiving a reward of zero due to a minor mistake 
    at the very end. Others may have performed incorrect reasoning from the outset—stemming from buggy file localization—making the entire trajectory something the model should not learn from.</p>

  <p>We approximate negative trajectory quality based on the <strong>ratio of wrong facts</strong> in the trajectory summary. A higher wrong ratio indicates a trajectory with little learning value. Negative trajectories with a wrong ratio of 80% or above are filtered out from the dataset.</p>

  <div class="table-wrap">
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr><th>Configuration</th><th>Avg Pass@1</th><th>Pass@3</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Positive trajectories only</td><td>53.95 ± 1.83</td><td>67.6</td></tr>
        <tr><td>+ ratio ≤ 0.25</td><td>55.93 ± 2.03</td><td>71.0</td></tr>
        <tr><td>+ ratio ≤ 0.5</td><td>56.63 ± 1.25</td><td>69.2</td></tr>
        <tr class="highlight-row"><td><strong>+ ratio ≤ 0.8</strong></td><td class="bold-row"><strong>58.05 ± 1.10</strong></td><td class="bold-row"><strong>70.4</strong></td></tr>
        <tr><td>+ ratio ≤ 1.0 (all negatives)</td><td>55.70 ± 0.83</td><td>69.4</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <!-- ── Analysis ── -->
  <h2>What Is Happening in the Model with Negative Data?</h2>

  <p>Our analysis reveals a two-stage effect of negative data with PI. Our analysis was computed on a single run, hence small differences from the averages in the above tables. 
    First, training on negative trajectories alone teaches the model <strong>exploration</strong>: 
    it learns to run more tests, backtrack when stuck, and recover from failed attempts—behaviors seen less often
    in positive-only training. This increased persistence directly translates to higher solve rates, 
    but at a cost: the model explores more broadly and takes longer to commit to a fix.</p>

  <p>Adding privileged information then acts as a <strong>focusing lens</strong>: because the model has seen ground-truth diagnostics explaining <em>why</em> a trajectory failed, it learns to localize bugs faster—cutting the number of steps before its first edit, reducing aimless exploration, and suppressing redundant verification loops—all while preserving the solve-rate gains from negative data.</p>

  <div class="callout-box">
    In short, <strong>negatives teach the model not to give up with diverse exploration</strong>, and <strong>PI teaches it where to look</strong>—yielding an agent that is both more resilient and more efficient.
  </div>

  <p>The table below breaks down this two-stage effect quantitatively across behavioral metrics. The first group captures overall performance; the second group (Effect 1: exploration) shows how negative trajectories increase thoroughness; the third group (Effect 2: focus) shows how PI then sharpens efficiency.</p>

  <!-- ── Transferability ── -->
  <hr class="section-rule" />

  <h2>Transferability to a Different Model Size</h2>

  <p>To test whether the effect holds at a different scale, we repeated the experiment 
    on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. The base mixture is from BugPilot <a href="#ref-bugpilot"> [Sonwane et al., 2025]</a>—25K 
    trajectories collected from two teacher models, Claude 4 <a href="#ref-claude4">[Anthropic, 2025]</a> and 
    MiniMax-M2.5 <a href="#ref-minimax">[MiniMax, 2025]</a>. To keep compute manageable, we trained for a single 
    epoch rather than the full three epochs of SFT training. On top of the base mixture we added positive or negative 
    trajectories at two budgets—roughly 3K and roughly 11K examples—and compared the two 
    datasets. We followed the same setup for the negative datasets: we filtered out trajectories with a wrong-fact ratio above 80% and added privileged information to the user prompt.
    We report the average Pass@1 resolution rate on SWE-bench Verified.</p>

  <div class="table-wrap">
    <table>
      <thead>
        <tr><th>Configuration</th><th>Dataset Size</th><th>Avg Pass@1</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Base mixture</td><td>25K</td><td>27.6 ± 1.41</td></tr>
        <tr><td>+ Positive</td><td>+ 3K</td><td>28.8 ± 0.51</td></tr>
        <tr class="highlight-row"><td><strong>+ Negative w PI</strong></td><td>+ 2.6K</td><td class="bold-row"><strong>29.2 ± 0.70</strong></td></tr>
        <tr><td>+ Positive</td><td>+ 11K</td><td>28.6 ± 0.99</td></tr>
        <tr class="highlight-row"><td><strong>+ Negative w PI</strong></td><td>+ 12K</td><td class="bold-row"><strong>30.4 ± 0.42</strong></td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <p>Two patterns from the main experiments reappear on the small model. First, adding positive data saturates: 
    going from 3K to 11K positives leaves Pass@1 essentially unchanged (28.8 → 28.6, within error), 
    consistent with the diversity ceiling seen earlier—once the added positives stop introducing 
    new tasks, more of them contribute little. Adding negatives does not saturate performance: negative trajectories with PI 
    improve the model from 29.2 at 2.6K to 30.4 at 12K. Second, at a comparable data budget, negative trajectories are at least as sample-efficient 
    as positive ones: at the smaller scale, negative trajectories match positive-only performance 
    while using fewer examples (29.2 vs. 28.8, within error; 2.6K vs. 3K), and at the larger scale, 
    it yields a clear improvement (30.4 vs. 28.6, non-overlapping error bars). The effect holds on a smaller model on top of the base 
    mixture built with enough positive trajectories.</p>
  
  
  <!-- ── Where Recent Works ── -->
  <h2>Related Work</h2>

  <h3>Code Agent Training</h3>

  <p>After SWE-agent <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793">[Yang et al., 2024]</a> introduced the Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) 
    for repository-level code editing, SWE-RL <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18449">[Wei et al., 2025]</a> trained coding agents 
    using RL over real GitHub issue and PR histories. A wave of follow-up work—SWE-smith <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.21798">[Yang et al., 2025]</a> and SWE-Fixer <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.05040">[Xie et al., 2025]</a>—achieved strong results on SWE-bench by training on large-scale demonstration data via SFT. However, all of these approaches discard failed rollouts and train exclusively on successful trajectories.</p>

  <h3>Learning from Negative Trajectories</h3>

  <p><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11651">Wang et al. [2024]</a> were among the first to show that failed trajectories 
    carry useful signal: simply prefixing training examples with a success/failure label yields large gains on math reasoning 
    and QA tasks. <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02502">Song et al. [2024]</a> proposed Trial and Error, 
    building contrastive pairs from failure trajectories and training with DPO in an iterative loop. 
    <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.20689">An et al. [2024]</a> explore whether LLMs can learn from mistakes (LEMA), 
    incorporating mistake-correction data pairs during fine-tuning. Taking this further, 
    <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13145">Lan et al. [2025]</a>, <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.15040">Peng et al. [2026]</a> 
    found that even expert failure trajectories contain helpful early steps—mistakes tend to occur only in the final few actions, 
    meaning the bulk of a failed rollout is still informative and able to improve the policy of the models. <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24517">Shrivastava et al. [2026]</a>
    also found that failed rollouts contain rich evidence about how the environment responds, which agents can learn from.</p>

  <h3>Learning from Feedback</h3>

  <p>Beyond binary success/failure labels, a parallel line of work uses richer feedback as a training signal. RLTF <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02482">[Song et al., 2026]</a> treats text feedback as an intermediate signal between sparse scalar rewards and expensive full demonstrations—richer than a binary label, yet cheaper to collect than complete expert trajectories. IXT <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20285">[Cui et al., 2025]</a> annotates training data with natural language critiques via a thinking reward model, then prefix-conditions the model on this feedback, achieving up to 2.8× compute efficiency. RLCF <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18624">[Viswanathan et al., 2025]</a> extracts instruction-specific checklists and scores each criterion individually to compute rewards for RL, outperforming standard alignment baselines. 
    π-Distill <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.04942">[Penaloza et al., 2026]</a> trains a privileged information-conditioned teacher and an unconditioned student jointly within the same model, transferring training-time privileged information to a policy that acts without it.
    Adding annotations to SFT data has also been shown to preserve the pretraining distribution and mitigate semantic mode collapse during fine-tuning <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.09995">[Springer et al., 2025]</a> .
  </p>

  <p>Our work builds on these threads. 
    Rather than labeling trajectories as simply pass or fail, we explicitly identify <em>which knowledge</em> within a failed coding trajectory was wrong and 
    inject it as privileged information in the prompt during SFT, so that the wrong information attends to the prompt and is not internalized into the model's parameters.</p>
